title: A WOMAN BLED NORMALLY—AND GOD GAVE ISRAEL LAWS ABOUT IT
paragraphs: A WOMAN BLED NORMALLY—AND GOD GAVE ISRAEL LAWS ABOUT IT

Leviticus 15 sounds uncomfortable until you understand what “unclean” actually meant. Then a bleeding woman reaches for Jesus—and suddenly the ancient law becomes part of one of the most breathtaking pictures of grace in the Gospel.
There are passages in the Bible we underline.
There are passages we quote when life falls apart.
And then there are passages we quietly turn past because we have absolutely no idea what to do with them.
Leviticus 15 is one of those passages.
Blood.
Bodily discharges.
Semen.
Menstruation.
Beds becoming unclean.
Chairs becoming unclean.
People washing themselves and waiting until evening.
It doesn't exactly sound like the verse you would print on a coffee mug.
But perhaps that is precisely why we need to read it.
Because buried inside this uncomfortable chapter is something many Christians have never been properly taught:
A woman's normal menstrual period had its own purity regulations under the covenant God gave ancient Israel.
And no...
that did not mean God considered women sinful because they menstruated.
It did not mean menstruation was a moral failure.
It did not mean a woman's body disgusted God.
And it certainly does not give Christians permission to treat women experiencing menstruation as spiritually inferior, shameful, contaminated, or somehow farther from God.
If you have ever read the word “unclean” in Leviticus and automatically heard “sinful,” what comes next may change the way you read an enormous portion of your Bible.
Listen to the Hebrew of Leviticus 15:19:
וְאִשָּׁה כִּי־תִהְיֶה זָבָה דָּם יִהְיֶה זֹבָהּ בִּבְשָׂרָהּ שִׁבְעַת יָמִים תִּהְיֶה בְנִדָּתָהּ וְכָל־הַנֹּגֵעַ בָּהּ יִטְמָא עַד־הָעָרֶב
Ve'ishah ki-tihyeh zavah, dam yihyeh zovah bivsarah, shiv'at yamim tihyeh beniddatah...

In context, the verse describes a woman experiencing a flow of blood and says that she remains in her נִדָּה — niddah state for seven days; one who touches her becomes טָמֵא — tamei, ritually impure, until evening.
That last distinction matters enormously.
Tamei is not another Hebrew word for “evil woman.”
Ritual impurity and moral guilt are not interchangeable categories.
We know this even from Leviticus 15 itself because the chapter does not begin with menstruation.
It begins with male bodily discharges.
Then the chapter discusses semen.
Leviticus 15:16 says that when a man has an emission of semen, he is to wash and remains ritually impure until evening.
Then comes something even more important.
Sexual intercourse itself could result in temporary ritual impurity for both the man and the woman, requiring washing and lasting until evening.
Then the chapter addresses a woman's normal menstrual bleeding.
Then it addresses prolonged or irregular bleeding.
Male.
Female.
Normal bodily processes.
Abnormal bodily conditions.
This is not a chapter written simply to humiliate women.
It belongs to an entire biblical system governing ritual purity and Israel's relationship to God's holy dwelling among them.
The chapter itself eventually tells us why these distinctions mattered:
“You shall put the Israelites on guard against their impurity... by defiling My Tabernacle which is among them.” — Leviticus 15:31
The sanctuary is central to the logic of the chapter.
God had chosen to dwell among His covenant people.
Holy space mattered.
Purity mattered.
Approaching God's dwelling mattered.
The ordinary Israelite lived in a world where holiness was not treated casually.
And that makes something else incredibly important:
Becoming ritually impure was not necessarily the same thing as committing a sin.
Sometimes impurity came through conditions and bodily processes that were simply part of embodied human existence.
A man could become ritually impure.
A woman could become ritually impure.
A person could become ritually impure without having committed some secret act of rebellion against God.
That distinction protects Leviticus 15 from a cruel interpretation Scripture itself does not require.
A menstruating woman was not being declared morally worthless.
She was not being told that being female was sinful.
She had entered a temporary ritual condition regulated within Israel's covenant life.
And then Leviticus makes another distinction that becomes extraordinarily important when we reach the New Testament.
Normal menstruation is addressed beginning in verse 19.
But Leviticus 15:25 describes something different: a woman whose bleeding continues for many days outside or beyond the expected time of menstruation.
Now hold that thought.
Because centuries later...
a woman begins walking through a crowd.
We don't know her name.
Mark simply tells us:
Καὶ γυνὴ οὖσα ἐν ῥύσει αἵματος δώδεκα ἔτη...
Kai gynē ousa en rhysei haimatos dōdeka etē...
“A woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years...”
Twelve.
Years.
Not seven days.
Not another monthly cycle.
Twelve years.
Mark 5 tells us that she had suffered greatly under many physicians. She had spent everything she possessed.
Instead of improving...
she became worse.
Try not to rush past that sentence.
Twelve years of waking up and realizing the bleeding had not stopped.
Twelve years of hoping this treatment might finally work.
Twelve years of disappointment.
Twelve years of watching money disappear.
Twelve years of carrying a condition nobody around her could simply pretend did not matter.
Leviticus 15:25–30 specifically addressed prolonged bleeding outside the normal menstrual period, including purification procedures after the discharge ceased.
So when the Gospel writers tell their original readers that this woman had experienced an ongoing flow of blood for twelve years, the language lands inside a world already shaped by Torah.
Suddenly this isn't merely a medical story.
There is a purity dimension hanging over the scene.
And she walks into a crowd anyway.
Maybe that is where this story stops being ancient history for you.
Because you know what it feels like to carry something for too long.
Maybe yours isn't blood.
Maybe it's shame.
Pornography nobody knows about.
A marriage quietly collapsing behind smiling photographs.
A child you cannot stop worrying about.
An addiction you keep promising God you will defeat.
A wound from childhood you learned to joke about because telling the truth hurts too much.
A prayer that has been unanswered so long that you have stopped telling people you're still praying it.
Church hurt.
Secret resentment.
Grief.
Fear.
A double life.
Maybe everyone around you thinks you're doing fine.
You learned when to smile.
You learned the Christian vocabulary.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know what worship song to post.
You know how to look spiritually alive while something inside you is hemorrhaging.
And perhaps the loneliest part is this:
Nobody can see the bleeding.
But you can.
She had been bleeding for twelve years.
And then she heard about Jesus.
That sentence changed everything.
She did not have another physician.
She did not have another payment.
She did not have another treatment plan.
She had Jesus.
So she moved through the crowd believing that if she could only touch His garment, she would be made well.
Imagine her hand shaking.
One more step.
Another body in the way.
Another step.
Then...
she touches Him.
And the bleeding stops.
Immediately.
But Jesus does something unexpected.
He stops too.
“Who touched My garments?”
The disciples almost sound bewildered.
Everybody is touching You.
Look at the crowd.
People are pressing against You from every direction.
But Jesus knew this touch was different.
Eventually the woman comes forward.
Mark says she is afraid and trembling.
She falls before Him.
And then Scripture gives us one of the most human sentences in the entire scene:
She told Him the whole truth.
Not the edited truth.
Not the church-friendly truth.
Not the version designed to preserve her reputation.
The whole truth.
Somebody reading this needs those four words.
Tell Jesus the whole truth.
Tell Him where you have fallen.
Tell Him what you keep hiding.
Tell Him what hurts.
Tell Him what you are ashamed of.
Tell Him about the anger.
Tell Him about the lust.
Tell Him about the doubt.
Tell Him about the bitterness.
Tell Him about the thing you swore you would never do again...
and did again.
He already knows.
Confession does not give an uninformed God new information.
It brings us out of hiding before the God who already sees us.
And listen carefully to the first word Jesus speaks to this trembling woman.
He does not say:
“Disgusting.”
He does not say:
“Problem.”
He does not even address her impersonally as “woman.”
He says:
Θυγάτηρ — Thygatēr.
Daughter.
Let that word sit there.
Daughter.
The woman who had been defined throughout the story by her bleeding is addressed by Jesus relationally.
Daughter.
Then He says:
ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
hē pistis sou sesōken se.
“Your faith has made you well.”
The verb translated “made you well” is σῴζω — sōzō, whose range can include saving, rescuing, delivering, or making whole depending on context.
Mark is describing genuine physical healing here; we should not flatten the story into a metaphor.
Her body was actually healed.
But Mark's language is still breathtaking.
Jesus does not merely stop a hemorrhage.
He publicly receives the trembling woman.
He calls her Daughter.
He sends her away in peace.
ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην — hypage eis eirēnēn.
Go in peace.
This is where we must be careful not to make the story say something it doesn't.
Jesus was not correcting Moses as though God's previous revelation had been evil.
He was not announcing that God's holiness had been a mistake.
The purity laws belonged to Israel's covenantal sanctuary system.
Jesus comes within Israel's story and brings it toward fulfillment.
And in Him, something astonishing keeps happening.
Jesus touches people others would avoid.
Jesus approaches the diseased.
Jesus touches lepers.
Jesus walks toward death.
And instead of impurity conquering Him...
His holiness brings cleansing, restoration, life.
That is where Leviticus begins pointing beyond itself.
Not because Leviticus was bad.
Because Leviticus taught Israel something modern people desperately want to forget:
God is holy.
We want grace without holiness.
Jesus without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Resurrection without a cross.
A Savior who comforts us but never confronts us.
But biblical grace is breathtaking precisely because biblical holiness is real.
Sin really does separate.
Guilt really does matter.
God really is holy.
And unlike menstrual impurity, sin is a moral problem.
That distinction cannot be blurred.
Your body functioning as God designed human biology to function is not the same thing as rebelling against God.
Menstruation is not a confession-worthy sin.
But pride is.
Lust is.
Hatred is.
Idolatry is.
Deception is.
Sexual immorality is.
Self-righteousness is.
Unbelief is.
Our deepest problem is not that we occasionally become socially unacceptable.
Our deepest problem is that sinners cannot make themselves righteous before a holy God.
And no amount of pretending can wash that away.
That is why Jesus did not merely come to give inspirational speeches.
He came to save sinners.
The Son of God took flesh.
He lived without sin.
He went willingly to the cross.
He bore sin.
He shed His blood.
He died.
And He rose.
The scandal of Christianity is not that respectable people can improve themselves if they follow Jesus' advice.
The scandal is that guilty people can be forgiven because Jesus Christ did for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves.
Grace does not say your sin doesn't matter.
Grace says your sin mattered enough for Christ to die...
and His love was great enough that He came anyway.
Maybe you have spent years trying to clean yourself up before approaching Jesus.
“I'll pray when I get myself together.”
“I'll return to church when I stop doing this.”
“I'll surrender after I fix my life.”
“I'll come back to God when I'm worthy.”
Listen.
You will die waiting to become worthy enough to need no Savior.
The bleeding woman did not heal herself and then touch Jesus.
She touched Jesus because she could not heal herself.
That does not mean faith is magic.

It does not mean every physical disease will disappear immediately when someone believes hard enough. Scripture does not authorize us to condemn suffering Christians as faithless simply because healing has not come.
The point is much greater.
Jesus is the One to whom helpless people may come.
And when it comes to the guilt of sin, the Gospel makes a promise far greater than temporary physical relief.
Christ receives repentant sinners.
Not because repentance purchases grace.
Not because tears impress God.
Not because you can compensate for yesterday.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Perhaps you have been hiding for twelve years in your own way.
Maybe twenty.
Maybe forty.
Maybe nobody knows.
Jesus does.
And the same Christ who made a trembling woman tell “the whole truth” already knows yours.
So stop negotiating.
Stop pretending.
Stop calling chains “personality.”
Stop renaming sin so you don't have to repent of it.
Stop trying to make darkness comfortable.
Bring the whole truth to Jesus.
Repent.
Believe the Gospel.
Ask Him for mercy.
There is forgiveness in Christ.
There is cleansing in Christ.
There is reconciliation in Christ.
There is no sin so fashionable that it stops being sin...
and there is no repentant sinner so scandalous that the blood of Christ suddenly becomes insufficient.
That is our heartbeat at Gospel Warrior.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing truth.
Jesus rewrites everything by taking sinners whose stories looked irredeemable and making grace the final word.
Peter denied Him.
Grace wasn't finished.
Paul persecuted His people.
Grace wasn't finished.
The thief was dying beside Him.
Grace wasn't finished.
And if you belong to Christ...
grace is not finished with you either.
Maybe this article exposed something you have kept hidden.
Don't perform for the comments.
Someone reading silently at two in the morning may need to know that Jesus still restores broken people.
If someone came to mind while you were reading this, don't just think about sending it.
Send it.
Send it privately to the person who would never comment publicly but desperately needs to hear that Christ still receives repentant sinners.
There may come a night when you need to read it again.
It doesn't.
Not because giving money buys a blessing.
It doesn't.
It shouldn't.
But voluntary, generous support of Gospel ministry is thoroughly biblical. Christians are called to generosity, and those who benefit from Gospel ministry may freely help sustain Gospel work.

So if you have been asking, “How can I help Gospel Warrior keep going, reach farther, create more biblical resources, and place Christ-centered truth in front of people who may never walk through a church door?”—this is one practical way.
And sharing costs you nothing.
A share helps carry the message.
Both can become practical acts of generosity when they are done freely, prayerfully, and for God's glory rather than human recognition.
We want Christ glorified, not people manipulated.
We want people reading Scripture.
Learning doctrine.
Repenting.
Healing.
Growing.
Praying.
Sharing Christ.
Becoming disciples who make disciples.
Not so we can build a crowd around a page.
So we can keep pointing a crowd toward Jesus.
Because one day likes disappear.
Algorithms change.
Pages disappear.
Possessions stay behind.
Our bodies return to dust.
But Christ remains.
And perhaps that is the lesson hiding inside an uncomfortable chapter about bodies, blood, purity, washing, separation, and the holy presence of God.
Human beings are fragile.
God is holy.
We cannot save ourselves.
And still...
He comes near.
The woman reached through the crowd thinking she needed only to touch His garment.
But Jesus stopped because He intended to give her something more than an anonymous miracle.
He called her Daughter.
Maybe you came to this article curious about menstruation in Leviticus.
Maybe you stayed because somewhere along the way you realized the person bleeding wasn't only her.
It was you.
Not physically.
Somewhere deeper.
Somewhere nobody sees.
And perhaps you have become very good at hiding the wound.
But Jesus already knows the whole truth.
You do not need another mask.
You need Christ.
So come out of hiding.
Repent where repentance is needed.
Receive grace where shame has been screaming.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Confess what needs confessing.
Seek help where help is needed.
And keep walking toward Jesus.
Because sometimes the person everyone else sees as a problem is only one encounter away from hearing Jesus speak a new name over the story.
She came trembling with twelve years of bleeding behind her—and walked away carrying one word no disease could take from her: Daughter.
